newsitem.title: USA: SEC approves Nasdaq-proposed lower quote size.
newsitem.headline: SEC approves Nasdaq-proposed lower quote size.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission said Thursday it approved a Nasdaq stock market proposal to reduce the number of shares that can be traded under new order handling rules that go into effect January 20.

The minimum limit order quote size will be cut to 100 shares, from the previous 1,000 shares. It will be applied on a pilot basis on the 50 most active stocks traded on the Nasdaq. Other Nasdaq-listed securiites will be phased in over the next eight months.

The rule changes approved will include a three-month pilot during which Nasdaq market makers will be able to quote minimum share sizes of at least 100 shares when they are not displaying customer limit orders.
A limit order is one in which customers specify the buy or sell price they wish to trade.
Currently, Nasdaq market makers are required to quote minimum sizes ranging from 200 to 1,000 shares, depending on the security.

The SEC said it approved the Nasdaq modifications to the order handling rules it approved in August "to address the changing role of Nasdaq market makers, now that individual and institutional limit orders will compete with market maker quotes."
The agency said the pilot period will give it a chance to assess the impact of the rule change on the market before considering whether or not to make it permanent.
Nasdaq, in a statement, applauded the SEC's action saying the change means quotes on the Nasdaq screen will now display both the price and size of "true buying and selling interest."
As this developed, a New York-based law firm criticized the SEC action "anti-consumer" and said it would go to court to challenge the SEC action.
Bill Singer, partner of the law firm Singer Zamansky LLP, said the firm had been authorized by its broker clients "to have the order enjoined."

SEC's order handling rules require Nasdaq market makers to display to the entire marketplace a customer's limit order that is priced at or better than their current quote. Also, better priced limit orders shown in private electronic trading systems will also be incorporated on Nasdaq screens.
